optionReasons.saa-med-029:option:0: It's the closest because VPC endpoint is exactly the solution — but the wrong type: Gateway Endpoints exist ONLY for S3 and DynamoDB; the services of the Systems Manager (ssm, ssmessages, ec2messages) require INTERFACE PrivateLink endpoints.

optionReasons.saa-med-029:option:2: Internet Gateway 'only for the SSM' does not exist — one IGW opens public route to the sub-network, violating the entire policy.

finalJustifications: Because the interface ends (PrivateLink) for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages create private ENIs in VPC: the agent reaches the Systems Manager without any route to the internet.
Because endpoint interfaces route traffic from SSM by a tunnel VPN managed up to AWS, encrypted off the public internet.
Because endpoints interfaces copy documents and patches from SSM within the VPC, applied locally without external communication.
Because endpoints interfaces release an exception to output in NAT of AWS only for the SSM, invisible to security policy.

optionReasons.saa-med-030:option:0: It is the closest because it removes the password from the configuration file, which is the apparent inconvenience — but only changes the hiding place: the password remains static, now recorded in a AMI (worse to rotate and visible to whom to launch the image); the requirement is temporary token via roll, which is the IAM database authentication.
optionReasons.saa-med-030:option:2: Using the master in all applications focuses the bank's highest privilege on shared credentials — the opposite of eliminating risks.
optionReasons.saa-med-030:option:3: Disable authentication for internal connections leaves the bank open to any process on the network — no serious option.

finalJustifications: Because IAM database authentication exchange password for tokens of 15 minutes issued based on the instance roll — temporary, rotating and secret file-free credentials.
Because IAM database authentication injects the bank password into the application memory via IMDS, without ever recording it on disk or configuration.
Because IAM database authentication rotates MySQL's fixed password daily, synchronizing the application configuration file.
Because IAM database authentication delegates the login to Secrets Manager, which validates the roll before releasing the bank's master credentials.

optionReasons.saa-med-031:option:2: Block Public Access protects buckets S3 against exposure — no relationship to root login.
optionReasons.saa-med-031:option:3: It is the closest because the credible report is a real practice of auditing credentials — but it is manual and weekly review: a root login would appear days later; the requirement of MINUTOS requires the event of the CloudTrail filtered by EventBridge with notification SNS.

finalJustifications: Because CloudTrail records the root ConsoleLogin, the rule of EventBridge filter this event in almost real time and the SNS notify team in minutes.
Because EventBridge blocks the root session until team confirmation, and the SNS deliver the request for approval of the suspicious login.
Because CloudTrail intercept the root password in the login and validate it against the safe before releasing the console for the session.
Because the rule of EventBridge deactivate or MFA of root after alert, forcing the new registry by legitimate administrator.

optionReasons.saa-med-034:option:0: Keeping as 'backup' preserves exactly the risk: program keys to active root are the most dangerous account credentials.
optionReasons.saa-med-034:option:1: Sharing root keys with whoever is multiplying exposure — there's never any justification for routine use of them.
optionReasons.saa-med-034:option:3: It is the closest because periodic rotation is the standard good practice for access keys COMUNS — but not for the root: the recommendation of the AWS is that the root simply DO NOT have access keys; rotating keeps alive a credential that should not exist.

finalJustifications: Because good practice is to eliminate: root should not have programmatic key accesses — excluding them removes the most powerful credentials and tasks migrate to identities IAM.
Because deleting keys automatically converts the scripts that used them to the admin roll, without any interruption.
Because exclusion triggers forced rotation of all account access keys, renewing the credentials park at once.
Because the root keys expire alone after 90 days of inactivity, and manual exclusion only anticipates the natural process.

optionReasons.saa-med-035:option:1: It is the closest because it also points to a real element of politics. IAM — but the Resource defines A QUAIS RNAs permission applies, not where the request comes from; context as IP of origin and MFA this is the role of the Condition element.
optionReasons.saa-med-035:option:2: Security Groups filter network traffic of resources like EC2 — do not attach to users or control the console.
optionReasons.saa-med-035:option:3: Tags categorize identities for organization and billing — do not impose contextual access restrictions.

finalJustifications: Because Condition assesses the context of each request: aws:SourceIp restricts the IPs of the office and aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent requires MFA in the sitting — the two requirements in one element.
Because Condition records the location of each login in CloudTrail, and the actions outside the office go in the team approval row.
Because Condition delegates IP validation to Security Group of VPC of the console, unifying the network and account identity rules.
Because Condition encrypts sessions started outside the office, allowing remote access with an extra layer of data protection.

finalJustifications: Because the dates of events of S3 no CloudTrail record operations at object level — GetObject included — with identity, time and IP of each access to the chart pocket.
Because the data events activate the log access within the object itself, which starts to load the reader's history in the metadata of S3.
Because the data events replicate each object read to an audit bucket, preserving the exact copy of what was accessed in the query.
Because data events demand MFA for the readings of the pocket, and each validation generates the record required by the health audit.

optionReasons.saa-med-038:option:0: SSE-S3 it's cryptography on the side of SERVIDOR with keys managed by AWS — the opposite of keeping the keys in the customer.
optionReasons.saa-med-038:option:1: It's the closest because the TLS also encrypts and protects the data on the way to AWS — But only IN THE WAY: upon arrival, the provider sees them clearly to store; encrypting before sending, with key that never leaves the client, is client-side encryption.
optionReasons.saa-med-038:option:3: Hashing is irreversible — card data could never be recovered again; hash is not encryption.

finalJustifications: Because in client-side encryption the application encrypts the data ANTES of sending with keys that remain in the customer — the AWS only stores the already encrypted material, never seeing the clear.
Because the client-side encryption negotiates with AWS an exclusive session key, used by the provider only to check the integrity of the shipments.
Because the client-side encryption divides the key into two halves between the client and the KMS, and none of the parts deciphers the card data alone.
Because the client-side encryption uses the TLS from tip to tip to final disk, extending the transit protection to the rest of the card data.

optionReasons.saa-med-033:option:0: Private channel of the team is not safe storage — the credentials continue in clear text in the function and now also spread in chats.
optionReasons.saa-med-033:option:2: Move to source code gets worse: the secret enters the Git repository and in each build, visible to anyone with access to code.
optionReasons.saa-med-033:option:3: It is the closest because it seems to reduce the exposure in the configuration — but Base64 is coding, not encryption: anyone decodes in a second; the credentials need to leave the function and live in the Secrets Manager, searched in runtime via IAM.

finalJustifications: Because Secrets Manager saves encrypted credentials and runtime search function via execution roll — exits visible configuration and gains rotation and audit.
Because Secrets Manager injects the described credential in the environment variable to each deployment, hiding it from the configuration.
Because Secrets Manager validates the signature of the function at each invocation, and only the authorized code receives the third party's credentials.
Because Secrets Manager replaces the credentials with a public alias, and the third resolves the real value in the first call of the API.
